title: Auth over HTTP: sessions, bearer tokens and JWTs
objectives: Trace how credentials travel in a cookie session and with a bearer access token, and say where the state lives in each
Decode a JWT's three parts by hand, and explain why a signed token is readable by anyone who holds it
Verify an access token the way a library does: pin the algorithm, check the signature, then `exp` in seconds
Answer with 401 + `WWW-Authenticate` or 403 per RFC 9110 and RFC 6750, and react to each as a client
Explain refresh-token rotation and reuse detection, and read `Set-Cookie` attributes as mechanics

sources.title: RFC 9700: OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice (refresh token rotation)

questions.prompt: In a cookie-session app, what puts the session id on each request to the API?

options.text: The browser, automatically, on requests that match the cookie's domain, path and other attributes
Your `fetch` wrapper, which copies it into a `Cookie` header
Your code, which reads it from `localStorage` and adds an `Authorization` header
The server, which appends it to every link it renders

questions.explanation: After `Set-Cookie`, the browser owns the cookie and attaches it to matching requests by itself — your code doesn't (and with `HttpOnly`, can't) touch it. A bearer token is the opposite: your code stores it and adds `Authorization: Bearer …` on every call. Which of the two is safer in a browser is a Web Security question; *who attaches it* is the mechanical difference.

questions.prompt: You ban a user. With server-side sessions their next request fails; with 15-minute JWT access tokens they keep working for up to 15 minutes. Why?

options.text: The JWT carries its own claims and is verified without a lookup, so it stays valid until `exp` unless you add a denylist check
Browsers cache JWTs and replay the old responses
A new signing key takes 15 minutes to propagate to all servers
TLS session resumption keeps the old identity alive

questions.explanation: A session id means nothing without its row in the store, so deleting the row revokes it instantly. A JWT is verified by checking its signature and `exp` — nothing asks "is this user still allowed?". That's the speed-for-revocation trade, and why access tokens are kept short, with revocation applied at the next refresh. Rotating the signing key would work, but it logs out *everyone*.

questions.prompt: A teammate puts the user's email and billing plan in the JWT payload: "it's fine, the token is encrypted with HS256". Is it?

options.text: No — the payload is base64url-encoded JSON. HS256 *signs* it; anyone holding the token can read it
Yes — HS256 encrypts the payload with the secret
Yes — decoding requires the server's secret
Yes — HTTPS encrypts it, so nobody else can read it

questions.explanation: A three-part JWT is a JWS: header and payload are just base64url, decodable with no key at all. The HMAC only proves nobody *changed* them. TLS protects the token in transit, but it is readable wherever it rests — browser storage, logs, a decoder pasted into by support. Encrypted JWTs (JWE) exist and have five parts; login endpoints almost never hand those out.

questions.prompt: A verifier runs `if (header.alg === "HS256" && !(await verifySignature(token))) reject();` and accepts anything else. What does an attacker send?

options.text: A token whose header says `"alg":"none"`, with any payload and an empty signature
A copy of a valid token captured earlier
Millions of HS256 tokens until one secret guess matches
Nothing works — the payload is signed

questions.explanation: The condition rejects only tokens that *claim* HS256 and fail. Claim anything else and the signature is never checked, so `{"sub":"admin"}` walks in. RFC 8725 lists exactly this (`alg: none`, and switching `RS256` to `HS256`). Pin the algorithm: reject unless the header is the one you issue *and* the signature verifies. Libraries like `jose` take an `algorithms` list for this reason.

questions.prompt: A valid, unexpired access token with `scope: "orders:read"` calls `DELETE /orders/7`, which needs `orders:write`. What should the API answer?

options.text: `403` with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="insufficient_scope"` (optionally naming the scope)
`401` with `error="invalid_token"`
`401` with no `WWW-Authenticate` header
`400` with `error="invalid_request"`

questions.explanation: The token proved who the caller is; the answer is still no. RFC 6750 maps `insufficient_scope` to `403`, and RFC 9110 says the client shouldn't retry `403` with the same credentials. `invalid_token`/`401` would send a well-behaved client off to refresh — and get the same scopes back, forever. A `401` must always carry `WWW-Authenticate`, and `invalid_request` is for malformed requests.

questions.prompt: Your single-page app gets `401` with `error="invalid_token"` on `GET /me`. What should it do?

options.text: Get a new access token (one shared refresh for all waiting calls), retry once, and send the user to log in if that still fails
Retry the same request with exponential backoff
Show "you don't have access to this"
Refresh and retry until the request succeeds

questions.explanation: `invalid_token` means the credential (usually an expired access token) is the problem, so a new one may fix it — but only once: if the fresh token fails too, something else is wrong. Retrying the same token gets the same `401`. "No access" is the `403` message. An unbounded refresh loop hammers the auth server, and with refresh-token rotation, parallel refreshes can trigger reuse detection.

questions.prompt: The server rotates refresh tokens and revokes the whole family when a used one comes back. Two tabs notice an expired access token and both call `/auth/refresh` with the same refresh token at the same moment. What happens?

options.text: One refresh succeeds; the other presents a just-used token, the server treats it as theft and revokes the family — the user is logged out
Both succeed; the server dedupes identical requests
Both receive the same new refresh token
The second request is ignored and the tab keeps its old token

questions.explanation: Reuse detection can't tell an attacker from your own second tab: a used refresh token arriving again means "two parties hold it", so per RFC 9700 the server revokes the active token too. The fix is on the client — make refreshing single-flight (and coordinate across tabs) so one refresh serves everyone waiting.

questions.prompt: `Set-Cookie: sid=9f2c1e; HttpOnly`. Which statement is true?

options.text: JavaScript can't read it through `document.cookie`, but the browser still sends it — including on `fetch` requests
It's sent on page navigations but never with `fetch`
It's only sent over HTTPS
It's only sent on requests from the same site

questions.explanation: `HttpOnly` controls *reading*, not *sending*: MDN notes the cookie "will still be sent with JavaScript-initiated requests". HTTPS-only is `Secure`; same-site-only is `SameSite=Strict`. Each attribute answers one question, which is why a sensitive cookie usually carries several.

prompts.prompt: The access token expired. Write the status code and the header a `401` must carry.
prompts.explanation: RFC 9110: a `401` MUST include `WWW-Authenticate` with at least one challenge. RFC 6750's `error="invalid_token"` tells the client the token itself is the problem — refreshing may help.

prompts.prompt: The token is fine; the user just isn't an admin.
prompts.explanation: RFC 6750's `insufficient_scope` goes with `403`, and the optional `scope` attribute names what would have been needed.

prompts.prompt: Reject the token from its expiry second on. `exp` is a NumericDate.
code: if (typeof claims.exp !== "number" || nowSeconds ___ claims.exp) return invalid;
prompts.explanation: `Date.now()` is milliseconds; `exp` is seconds since the epoch (RFC 7519). The token must not be accepted "on or after" `exp`, so the comparison is `>=`.

prompts.prompt: Keep the refresh token away from scripts, and send it only to the `/auth` endpoints.
prompts.explanation: `HttpOnly` hides the cookie from `document.cookie` (it is still sent); `Path=/auth` limits which URLs it's sent to. `Secure` and `SameSite=Strict` restrict *how* and *from where* it's sent.

prompts.prompt: With `jose` v6, pin the accepted algorithm and the intended audience.
prompts.explanation: `algorithms` stops the token's own header from choosing how it's checked (and `jose` never accepts `alg: none`). `audience` rejects a correctly signed token that was minted for a different API.

code: // The payload segment of a token for a user named "Zoë"
snippets.question: What happens?
acceptable: an exception — the _ isn't valid base64
snippets.explanation: JWT segments are base64**url**: `-` and `_` replace `+` and `/`. `atob` only accepts the classic alphabet, so the `_` in `Wm_D` throws a `DOMException` named `InvalidCharacterError`. Most tokens happen to decode — it depends on the bytes — so code that "worked in testing" breaks for some users. (Run in Node 24.)

snippets.question: The alphabet is fixed. What name is logged?
snippets.explanation: `atob` returns a "binary string" — one character per **byte**. `ë` is two bytes in UTF-8 (`0xC3 0xAB`), which come back as the two characters `Ã` and `«`. Turn the string into bytes and decode them as UTF-8: `new TextDecoder().decode(Uint8Array.from(atob(base64), c => c.charCodeAt(0)))` gives `Zoë`.

snippets.question: Roughly when does the verifier first reject this token as expired?
snippets.answer: Effectively never — read as seconds, exp is in the year 58,763
acceptable: in tens of thousands of years
snippets.explanation: The issuer wrote milliseconds into a claim that RFC 7519 defines in **seconds**. The verifier is correct, so it reads `1792220194000` seconds: `new Date(exp * 1000)` is in the year 58,763. Every token from this issuer is valid for good — and nothing errors. When a check involves `exp`, `iat` or `nbf`, look at the units on both sides.
